title: Typed DOM queries and events; forms and validation
summary: TypeScript's DOM types come from strings: tag names and event names map to precise types. Everything else is Element or EventTarget, which you narrow with instanceof, not as. Forms validate natively; you add rules and messages.

examples.title: Typed queries: tag names, instanceof, and the lying type argument

annotations.note: querySelector has one overload per tag name (HTMLElementTagNameMap in lib.dom.d.ts), so "form" returns HTMLFormElement | null and .elements is available once null is ruled out.
An id or class selector is just a string to tsc, so the result is Element | null: two problems, null and a type without value or valueAsNumber.
instanceof narrows Element to HTMLInputElement with a real runtime check. If someone changes the markup, the branch is skipped instead of failing somewhere later.

The type argument is a cast in disguise: tsc doesn't check it, and neither does the browser. #title is an h1, so value is undefined while the type says string. `as HTMLInputElement` lies the same way.
Pass the constructor and let instanceof do the check: el instanceof type narrows to T. The error says what was expected and what was found, at startup rather than in a later TypeError.
querySelectorAll("li") is NodeListOf<HTMLLIElement>: iterable and indexable, with forEach but no map, so spread it into an array. toLocaleUpperCase("tr") gives İZMİR, not IZMIR.

examples.title: Event maps, delegation, custom events, and removal by signal

annotations.note: One guard at the top removes null for the rest of the module: list is HTMLUListElement and filter is HTMLInputElement, inside callbacks too.

Event delegation: one listener on the list handles clicks on any row, including rows added later. e.target is the innermost node clicked and is typed EventTarget | null, so narrow it before calling closest().
Assigning .value fires no input event; only user actions do. Code and tests that set values must dispatch the event themselves, which is what testing libraries' user-event helpers do for you.

Declaration merging into HTMLElementEventMap types the custom event at every addEventListener: e.detail.plate is a string. dispatchEvent is not checked against the map, so keep the detail shape in one place.
The signal option removes the listener when the controller aborts. One controller can remove a whole group of listeners in a cleanup function. "keydown" maps to KeyboardEvent, so e.key is typed.

examples.title: Constraint validation, a custom rule, and FormData

annotations.note: The rules live in the markup: required, type="email", min and max. The browser checks them; no library needed for the basics.
Destructuring the typed NodeList gives three HTMLInputElements. tsc can't know how many inputs the markup has, so this is the line that breaks silently if the form changes.
ValidityState has a flag per rule. validationMessage comes in the browser's language, so a Turkish UI on an English browser shows English text: map the flags to your own messages.

setCustomValidity("message") makes the field invalid; "" makes it valid again, and nothing clears it for you. "izmir" upper-cased with the tr locale is İZMİR and matches; toUpperCase() would give IZMIR.

preventDefault stops the browser from submitting and navigating. checkValidity() runs every rule and fires invalid events without showing the browser's bubbles (reportValidity() shows them). FormData.get returns string | File | null: narrow before use.
On a real page, form.requestSubmit() validates and fires submit like a click on the submit button. The lesson sandbox lacks allow-forms, so the example dispatches the event itself.

use_cases: Pages and widgets without a framework: admin tools, embeds, browser extensions
Long or dynamic lists: one delegated listener instead of one per row
Forms that need required, type, min/max or pattern checks plus a few business rules
Inside React, refs give you these same typed elements and native APIs
strengths: lib.dom.d.ts types the DOM for free: tag names map to element types and event names to event types, so most handlers need no annotations
instanceof is a checked narrowing; a Java cast is checked at run time too, but TypeScript's as and type arguments are erased and check nothing
Native constraint validation and FormData handle most forms without a dependency, with messages already localized by the browser
weaknesses: Only tag-name selectors are typed; ids, classes and attribute selectors return Element, and the generic overload is an unchecked cast
Markup and code are checked separately: renaming an id breaks at run time, not at compile time (JSX closes that gap)
Native validation bubbles are hard to style, and their language is the browser's, not your app's

pitfalls.title: Casting query results
pitfalls.detail: as and querySelector<T> silence the compiler and check nothing. Narrow with instanceof and fail with a clear message.
pitfalls.good:
const email = document.querySelector("#email");
if (!(email instanceof HTMLInputElement)) throw new Error("#email missing");

pitfalls.title: Treating e.target as the element with the listener
pitfalls.detail: target is the innermost node that received the event, such as a span inside the button. Use closest() for delegation, or the variable you attached the listener to.

pitfalls.title: Expecting value assignment to fire events
pitfalls.detail: Setting .value or .checked from code fires neither input nor change. Dispatch the event if listeners must react.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting to clear setCustomValidity
pitfalls.detail: A non-empty custom message keeps the field invalid forever. Recompute it on every input and set "" when the value is fine.

pitfalls.title: Trusting client-side validation
pitfalls.detail: Anyone can skip it with devtools or curl. It is for the user's convenience; the server validates again.

quiz.q: What is the type of document.querySelector(".price")?
quiz.why: Only bare tag names select a typed overload. A class selector returns Element | null.

quiz.q: const el = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("#title"), and #title is an h1. What happens?
options: It compiles, and el.value is undefined at run time
quiz.why: The type argument is unchecked; the browser returns the h1, which has no value property.

quiz.q: Code sets input.value = "x". Does an input listener run?
options: No; only user-initiated changes fire input, so dispatch the event yourself
quiz.why: MDN: setting value programmatically does not fire input. Testing tools simulate typing to get real events.

quiz.q: How do you make a field fail checkValidity() because of your own rule?
quiz.why: validity is read-only; setCustomValidity sets the customError flag and the message, and "" clears them.

body:
## Concept

TypeScript ships the DOM's types in `lib.dom.d.ts`, and they are driven by strings. A
tag name passed to `querySelector`, `querySelectorAll`, `createElement` or `closest` picks
a precise element type through `HTMLElementTagNameMap`; an event name passed to
`addEventListener` picks the event type through the event maps (`"keydown"` gives a
`KeyboardEvent`). Anything the compiler cannot see, such as ids, classes or the actual
markup, comes back as `Element` or `EventTarget`. You then **narrow** with `instanceof`, a
real runtime check, instead of asserting with `as`.

Forms add a second built-in system: **constraint validation**. Attributes declare rules,
`validity` reports which ones fail, `setCustomValidity` adds your own, and `FormData`
collects the values as `string | File`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS**: the same API. TypeScript adds the `null` checks and the narrowing that
  jQuery-era code skipped.
- **Java/Android**: `findViewById<T>` and `(EditText) view` are checked at run time and
  throw on a mismatch. TypeScript's `as` and `querySelector<T>` are erased and check
  nothing; `instanceof` is the checked form.
- **Go**: server-rendered pages (`html/template`) validate on the server only. Client-side
  validation is a convenience on top; the Go handler must still validate (see the JSON
  validation lesson).
- **Python**: BeautifulSoup's `select()` returns untyped tags. Here the type follows the
  selector when it is a tag name, and stops at `Element` otherwise.

## How it works

An event travels in three phases: **capture** from the window down to the target's
parent, **target**, then **bubble** back up. Listeners run in the bubble phase unless
registered with `{ capture: true }`. Delegation depends on bubbling, so it only works for
events that bubble: `click` and `input` do, `focus` doesn't (use `focusin`), and a
`CustomEvent` only bubbles when created with `bubbles: true`.

`e.target` is where the event started; `e.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is
running. TypeScript types both as `EventTarget | null`, because one listener function can
be attached to anything.

## Design notes

Query and narrow once, at the edge of the program, then pass typed elements inward:
a helper like `must(selector, HTMLInputElement)` turns a markup mistake into one clear
error at startup. The rest of the code never sees `null` or `Element`.

Use native validation for the rules HTML already knows, `setCustomValidity` for business
rules, and your own message table so the language matches your UI rather than the
browser's. Treat it as user experience, never as security: the server repeats every check.
When the UI grows, JSX (the React lessons) closes the remaining gap, because markup and
code are type-checked together.
